beats.text: In under five minutes, a chip the size of a postage stamp finished a calculation that would take one of the world's fastest supercomputers ten septillion years.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: Frontier: one of the fastest supercomputers

beats.text: That's a one followed by twenty-five zeros. Far longer than the universe has existed.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The chip is Google's Willow, a quantum computer. And it sounds like magic, which is exactly why so much of what you hear about quantum computing is wrong.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So in the next few minutes, let's decode what a quantum computer really is, why it has to be colder than outer space, what it can and can't do, and why your bank is already preparing for it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Start with the computer you're using right now. Everything it does comes down to bits, tiny switches that are either zero or one.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Every photo, every video, every message is just billions of those switches flipping on and off, extremely fast.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: A quantum computer uses qubits instead. And a qubit can be in a mix of zero and one at the same time, a state called superposition.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: A simple way to picture it: a normal bit is a coin lying flat, heads or tails. A qubit is a coin still spinning in the air. Only when you look does it land on one side.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Qubits can also be linked together, so that measuring one instantly tells you something about another. That's called entanglement.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Here's why that matters. Two qubits can hold a blend of four possibilities. Ten can hold over a thousand. Three hundred qubits can hold more possibilities than there are atoms in the observable universe.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

rows: 300 qubits → more than atoms in the universe

els.by: THE MATHS (2 TO THE POWER OF n)

beats.text: Now, the most common explanation you'll hear is that a quantum computer tries every answer at the same time. That's the myth.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: "A quantum computer tries every answer at the same time"
els.hi: every answer at the same time

beats.text: If it simply tried everything at once, you'd still only get one random answer when you look. That's useless.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The real trick is called interference. Like waves in water, the possibilities can add up or cancel out.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: A quantum algorithm is a clever recipe that makes the wrong answers cancel each other out, and the right answer get stronger, so that when you finally measure, you're likely to see the right one.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: That's also why quantum computers aren't faster at everything. They only win on problems where someone has found a recipe like that.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: they win only where a recipe exists

beats.text: So why does a quantum computer look like a giant golden chandelier?
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Because qubits are incredibly fragile. The tiniest bit of heat, vibration or stray signal knocks them out of their delicate state. Physicists call this noise.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So most quantum chips, including Google's, sit inside special refrigerators that cool them to around ten thousandths of a degree above absolute zero.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Deep space is about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero. So the inside of a quantum computer is roughly two hundred and seventy times colder than outer space.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.source: Dilution refrigerators run at ~10 millikelvin (MIT, Bluefors)

beats.text: Even when they're that cold, qubits make mistakes. A lot of them. That's been the biggest wall in quantum computing for decades.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The fix is called error correction: you combine many physical qubits into one reliable "logical" qubit, so the group can catch and correct individual mistakes.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The problem was that adding more qubits usually added more errors too.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Willow's real breakthrough wasn't that five-minute race. It's that as Google made its groups of qubits bigger, the error rate went down instead of up. That's a key milestone researchers had been chasing for almost thirty years.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And in twenty twenty-five, Google showed an algorithm called Quantum Echoes running thirteen thousand times faster than one of the best supercomputers, on a result other machines can check.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.sub: and other machines can check it

beats.text: So what will quantum computers actually be useful for? Not for browsing, gaming or running ChatGPT faster.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Their best targets are problems that are quantum by nature. Simulating molecules to design new medicines, better batteries and new materials.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: They may also help with certain hard optimisation and simulation problems, though researchers are still debating how big that advantage will be.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And then there's the one that worries governments and banks: breaking the encryption that protects almost everything online.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Much of today's online security, from your UPI payments to your WhatsApp messages, relies on maths problems that normal computers would take practically forever to crack.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: A large enough, error-corrected quantum computer could solve some of those problems dramatically faster.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Nobody has built that machine yet. Official estimates put it somewhere in the twenty-thirties, and nobody knows the exact date.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.source: Industry summaries of official estimates (CSA, Palo Alto Networks)

beats.text: But there's a catch called "harvest now, decrypt later". Someone can steal encrypted data today and simply wait for a quantum computer to unlock it years from now.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: That's why in twenty twenty-four, the US standards agency NIST published the first "post-quantum" encryption standards, and set a plan to phase out vulnerable encryption after twenty thirty.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Tech companies and banks have already started switching. If your apps update their security quietly over the next few years, this is one big reason why.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: India is in this race too. In twenty twenty-three, the government approved the National Quantum Mission, with six thousand and three crore rupees over eight years.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The goal is to build quantum computers with up to a thousand qubits by around twenty thirty-one.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Today, one of India's most powerful machines, built by the Bengaluru startup QpiAI, has twenty-five qubits. That's far smaller than Google's, but it's a start.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: far smaller, but it's a start

beats.text: And India is ahead on quantum-secure communication, with more than a thousand kilometres of quantum-secure links already set up.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So, will you ever have a quantum computer at home? Almost certainly not. They're huge, fragile and built for very specific problems.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Instead, you'll use them the way you use most powerful computers today: through the cloud, often without even knowing it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Some companies already let students and developers run small programs on real quantum chips online, many for free.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Quantum computers won't replace your laptop. They'll work alongside regular computers, as special tools for a few incredibly hard problems.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: a special tool, not a replacement

beats.text: So, a quantum computer isn't a faster laptop, and it doesn't try every answer at once. It's a completely different machine, using the strange rules of physics to solve a few problems no normal computer ever could.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The hype is real in some places, and wildly overblown in others. Now you know which is which.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Tell me in the comments: what problem would you want a quantum computer to solve first?
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And subscribe to TechDecoded with Max for more tech, decoded.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace
